title: AI for Insurance — Underwriting, Claims & Fraud

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

Lesson 16-13 covered AI in regulated professions broadly — legal and healthcare — as an example of AI adoption under heavy compliance pressure. This lesson is the insurance-specific version of that story, and it's moved fast enough in 2026 that it deserves its own treatment: underwriting timelines that used to take days now take minutes at leading carriers, a named production deployment at AIG built with Anthropic and Palantir, and a genuinely new problem on the claims side — AI-powered photo and document editing making fraud both easier to commit and harder to catch. This lesson covers both halves: the underwriting speed-up, and the claims-fraud arms race it's now tangled up with.

## From Days to Minutes: Underwriting's 2026 Inflection Point

The headline number across multiple 2026 industry reports is dramatic: underwriting timelines that used to run 3-5 days are now completing in as little as 3-12 minutes at leading carriers, and straight-through processing rates (policies issued with no manual underwriter touch) have jumped from a historical 10-15% to 70-90% on standard products. One named example: Hiscox reports a production result of 3 minutes from submission to a bindable quote using AI pricing models that apply consistent rate logic across every submission with fully auditable adjustment rules.

But 'AI is transforming underwriting' and 'most insurers have actually transformed' are two different claims, and the gap between them is real. A BCG analysis found only 7% of insurers have achieved enterprise-wide AI transformation, despite near-universal AI investment — and separately, 82% of insurers say AI will define their industry's future while only 14% report having it fully integrated. Industry consensus for 2026 is that the era of small pilot programs is genuinely over — carriers still running pure proof-of-concept projects are considered behind, not cautious — but 'over' means most insurers are now mid-transition, not finished.

## AIG's Production Deployment: Claude, Palantir, and Multi-Agent Orchestration

The most-cited real production example in 2026 is AIG. Under CEO Peter Zaffino, AIG built what's now called **AIG Underwriter Companion**, combining three vendors for three distinct jobs: **Anthropic's Claude** provides the reasoning and dialogue layer, **Palantir Foundry** supplies the underlying ontology — a structured digital map connecting policies, exposures, and historical losses — and **Salesforce** handles the broker-facing workflow. The system reads incoming submissions, surfaces coverage gaps, and asks the next question a senior underwriter would ask, automating the routine triage work that previously consumed the most underwriter time. AIG reports underwriters now spend an estimated 50%+ less time on data ingestion and submission triage, freeing that time for the judgment calls that actually price risk.

In May 2026, AIG extended this from individual use cases into **multi-agent orchestration** across front-office underwriting, mid-office operations, and back-office functions — deploying **knowledge assistants** (real-time retrieval of loss history, comparable accounts, and jurisdiction-specific regulatory requirements the moment an underwriter opens a submission) alongside **adviser agents** (surfacing comparable historical accounts and pricing recommendations based on what's worked or failed on similar risks in the past). CEO Zaffino has pointed to the pace of change itself as notable: when AIG began working with an early Claude model, its agents could operate autonomously for under an hour; by 2026, they can run autonomously for up to 30 hours. On the claims side specifically, AIG reports an 88% AI-adjuster agreement rate — a useful early signal, though the longer-tail question of whether this holds up as claims mature over several accident years is still an open one.

**This is happening inside a tightening regulatory frame, not a lawless one.** As of Q1 2026, the NAIC's Model Bulletin on AI use in insurance has been adopted by 23 states plus Washington, D.C. — insurers are now required to document how AI-driven underwriting and claims decisions are made, maintain audit trails, and be able to explain a decision, not just produce one. The EU AI Act separately classifies insurance underwriting AI as 'high-risk,' triggering its strictest compliance requirements for any insurer operating in the EU. The operating model that's actually working, per industry analysis: a continuous human-AI hybrid where AI handles intake triage, document extraction, and risk scoring on standard products, while humans focus specifically on complex risks, exceptions, and governance oversight — carriers that designed this human-AI division of labor before deploying tools are reportedly the ones closing the transformation gap fastest; carriers that deployed tools first and hoped an operating model would follow are the ones stuck in what one analysis calls 'pilot purgatory.'

## The Other Side: AI-Powered Photo Editing Is Reshaping Claims Fraud

While underwriting AI speeds up the front end of an insurance relationship, a parallel and less flattering AI story is unfolding on the claims side. Verisk's **2026 State of Insurance Fraud Study** (published March 2026, surveying 1,000 U.S. consumers and 300 claims professionals) found that **98% of insurers say AI editing tools are fueling digital fraud** — yet only **32% feel very confident detecting deepfakes**, a striking confidence gap given how universally the problem is acknowledged. Three-quarters of insurers (76%) say manipulated media submissions have grown more sophisticated, two-thirds (66%) believe digital media fraud goes undetected often or very often industry-wide, and 99% say they've personally encountered manipulated or AI-altered documentation in a claim.

On the consumer side, the numbers are just as striking: more than a third of consumers (36%) said they'd consider digitally altering a claim photo or document even knowing it would break their insurer's rules — a figure that rises to 55% among Gen Z respondents specifically. Of consumers who've actually used AI editing tools to modify a claim-related photo, 44% described the results as 'very realistic.' Not every edit is fraud in the same sense, though — a slim majority of respondents (52%) considered brightness/contrast adjustment acceptable and 49% considered cropping out irrelevant background acceptable, while only small minorities condoned exaggerating damage (15%) or fabricating damage that never occurred (13%) — suggesting most people draw a real line, even as a meaningful minority don't.

**Insurers are responding with more friction, not less — and that friction will likely land on honest claimants too.** On the detection side, 65% of insurers now use automated, AI-based detection tools from third-party vendors, and half report using internally developed detection tools of their own — but given only 32% feel confident detecting deepfakes, this is very much an active arms race, not a solved problem. Looking ahead, insurers themselves expect the practical consequences to spread beyond catching fraudsters: 45% anticipate tighter documentation and proof-of-loss requirements for every claimant (not just suspected fraud cases), 35% expect longer claim-cycle times, and 35% expect higher premiums industry-wide as a result. If you file an insurance claim in the next few years, expect more friction and more documentation requests than you're used to — not because you're suspected of fraud specifically, but because the whole system is recalibrating around AI-editable photo evidence it can no longer take at face value.

sections.title: Workshop 1 — Research Your Own Insurer's AI Underwriting or Claims Stance
sections.content:
**Step 1 — Pick one policy you actually hold** (auto, home, renters, health) and identify your insurer.

**Step 2 — Research what you can find about that insurer's AI use.** Search '[your insurer] AI underwriting' and '[your insurer] AI claims 2026' — look for press releases, news coverage, or a page on their site describing automated underwriting or claims processing. Many insurers now disclose this, at least at a high level, given the NAIC disclosure requirements described in this lesson.

**Step 3 — Find your state's regulatory status.** Check whether your state has adopted the NAIC Model Bulletin on AI in insurance (search '[your state] NAIC AI model bulletin insurance 2026') — this tells you whether your insurer is currently required to document and explain AI-driven decisions that affect you specifically.

**Step 4 — Write a short personal note**: if your insurer denied a claim or priced a policy in a way you didn't understand, and you suspected an AI system was involved in that decision, what would you actually ask for? (Given the audit-trail and explainability requirements this lesson covered, 'explain how this decision was made' is a legitimate request in a Model-Bulletin state, not an unreasonable one.)

**Outcome:** a real, researched understanding of your own insurer's AI posture and your state's regulatory protections — plus a concrete question you're prepared to ask if an AI-influenced decision on your own policy or claim ever seems wrong.

sections.question: AIG's Underwriter Companion combines three different vendors. What does each one specifically contribute, according to this lesson?
options: All three vendors provide the same redundant AI model for reliability

Anthropic's Claude provides reasoning and dialogue, Palantir Foundry supplies the underlying ontology connecting policies, exposures, and historical losses, and Salesforce handles the broker-facing workflow
Palantir provides the AI model, Anthropic provides the data infrastructure, and Salesforce provides regulatory compliance
Only Anthropic is actually involved; Palantir and Salesforce are legacy systems being replaced
sections.explanation: This lesson describes a specific three-way division of labor: Claude (Anthropic) for reasoning/dialogue, Palantir Foundry for the structured ontology linking policies/exposures/losses, and Salesforce for the broker-facing workflow layer. Option C swaps the vendors' actual roles. Option D is wrong — all three are actively combined, not being phased out; that's the entire point of the multi-agent orchestration AIG built in 2026.

sections.title: Workshop 2 — Build Your Personal Claims-Documentation Habit for an AI-Skeptical Claims Environment
sections.content:
Given that insurers are tightening documentation requirements industry-wide (per this lesson's Verisk data), this workshop has you build a real habit that protects you as an honest claimant in that environment — before you ever need to file a claim under pressure.

**Step 1 — Pick one real policy** (home, renters, auto) where a future claim is plausible.

**Step 2 — Design your baseline documentation habit.** What would you photograph or video today, before any damage occurs, to have an unambiguous 'before' record? (A walkthrough video with a visible date/timestamp is generally more resistant to a 'was this AI-edited' suspicion than a single edited-looking photo.)

**Step 3 — Design your at-the-time-of-claim habit.** If you needed to file a claim tomorrow, what would you do differently now that you know 65% of insurers use automated fraud-detection tools and adjusters are increasingly trained to scrutinize digital media? (Original file formats with metadata intact, multiple angles, avoiding any editing app entirely — even a 'harmless' brightness adjustment — before submission.)

**Step 4 — Ask Claude or ChatGPT**: "Here's my claims-documentation plan: [paste Steps 2-3]. Given that insurers are increasingly scrutinizing digital claim photos for AI editing, what am I missing that could get an honest claim flagged by mistake?"

**Step 5 — Save this as a real personal reference note**, and if practical, actually take the baseline 'before' photos/video from Step 2 today rather than only planning to.

**Outcome:** a real, usable documentation habit — and possibly real baseline photos/video already taken — that protects you from being wrongly caught up in the fraud-detection friction this lesson described, the next time you actually need to file a claim.

sections.question: Verisk's 2026 study found 98% of insurers say AI editing tools are fueling fraud, but only 32% feel very confident detecting deepfakes. What does this specific combination best illustrate?
options: Insurers are exaggerating the problem to justify raising premiums

Widespread recognition of a threat doesn't automatically come with an equally mature ability to counter it — insurers agree almost universally that AI-edited claims are a real problem, but detection capability lags far behind that recognition, which is why 65% now rely on third-party AI detection tools rather than in-house confidence alone
The 98% figure is a measurement error and should be disregarded
Deepfake detection is impossible, so insurers have given up on it entirely
sections.explanation: This is the core tension the lesson highlights: near-universal problem recognition (98%) paired with low detection confidence (32%) describes an active, unresolved arms race, not a solved or fabricated problem. That's exactly why insurers are leaning on third-party detection vendors (65%) and internally developed tools (50%) simultaneously rather than trusting either their own confidence or one detection method alone. Option A isn't supported by the data cited. Option C dismisses a well-sourced survey finding without basis. Option D contradicts the lesson directly — insurers are actively investing in detection, not giving up.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 16-22 — and Part 16.** You now know the 2026 shift in insurance underwriting from pilot to production (days-to-minutes timelines, AIG's named Claude/Palantir/Salesforce deployment, and the human-AI hybrid operating model most successful carriers use), the tightening regulatory frame around it (NAIC Model Bulletin adoption, the EU AI Act's high-risk classification), and the parallel claims-fraud arms race driven by AI photo/document editing — where insurer confidence in detecting fraud lags far behind how universally they recognize the problem. You've researched your own insurer's AI posture and built a real documentation habit to protect yourself as an honest claimant. Part 17 begins next, covering project-work skills that apply across any role or industry.

sections.title: Turn a Real Claim File Into a Structured Summary & Risk-Flag Report
sections.content:
You're going to take a real (or realistic) insurance claim or policy file and use AI to produce the kind of structured summary and risk-flag report an adjuster or underwriter reviews before making a decision — the same first-pass work AIG's Underwriter Companion performs automatically, done here by hand with a mandatory licensed-professional verification step, since this lesson's entire second half is about why that step can't be skipped.

**Step 1 — Get your raw claim or policy file.** If you work in insurance and have access to a real (anonymized) claim file, submission, or policy application, use it. If you don't, ask Claude or ChatGPT to generate a realistic sample first: `"Generate a realistic auto or homeowners insurance claim file — incident description, claimant statement, an adjuster's initial notes, a repair estimate, and 2-3 details that are minor inconsistencies (not necessarily fraud, just the kind of thing that needs a closer look), written the way a real claim file actually reads (not overly clean)."`

**Step 2 — Paste the raw claim file into Claude or ChatGPT and ask:**
```
Here is a raw insurance claim file: [paste your file]

Turn this into a structured summary and risk-flag report with these sections:
1. Summary — incident type, claimed amount, key facts in 3-4 sentences
2. Consistency check — any details across the statement, notes, and estimate
   that don't line up, each with a one-line description of the discrepancy
3. Risk flags — anything that warrants a closer look (timing, documentation
   gaps, amount relative to typical claims of this type), clearly labeled as
   flags to investigate, not conclusions of wrongdoing
4. A mandatory "flag for licensed adjuster/underwriter verification" section
   listing every flag and inconsistency that requires human confirmation
   before any decision is made

Format as a report a reviewing adjuster or underwriter could work from directly.
```

**Step 3 — The mandatory adversarial review.** Paste the report back and ask: `"Find 3 specific problems with this report — places where a 'risk flag' is really just an ordinary, innocent explanation being treated as suspicious, or where the language implies fraud or wrongdoing rather than simply flagging something to verify."` Fix at least one before finalizing — given this lesson's data on false-positive fraud flags and equity concerns, language precision here isn't optional.

**Step 4 — Save the report as a reusable template**, and treat the licensed-professional verification section as non-negotiable every time you reuse it — this report is a first-pass triage aid, never a final coverage or fraud determination.

**Your deliverable:** a real, human-reviewed claims-file summary and risk-flag report with a mandatory licensed-adjuster/underwriter verification section — a genuine triage artifact, not a final determination.
